summary.text: A capsid is the protein shell of a virus, and it encloses the virus's genetic material.
Most viruses have a helical or icosahedral capsid, although some, such as bacteriophages, have more complicated structures.
Some viruses are enveloped, meaning the capsid is coated with a lipid membrane that it acquires from a cellular membrane of the host.

facts.label: Nucleocapsid
facts.value: The capsid and core together bear this name

facts.label: Icosahedral shape
facts.value: Twenty equilateral triangular faces, close to a sphere

facts.label: Foot-and-mouth capsid
facts.value: Faces made of three proteins, VP1 to VP3

items.prompt: A virologist sees a capsid with 20 triangular faces that nearly forms a ball. How is it described?

options.label: Helical, a shape like a spring
Icosahedral, a shape approximating a sphere
Enveloped, because of a lipid coat
Filamentous, like a loose thread

items.explain: The icosahedral shape has 20 equilateral triangular faces and approximates a sphere; the helical shape resembles a spring.

items.prompt: Some viruses wear an extra lipid coat over their protein shell. Where does that coat come from?

options.label: The virus builds it from scratch with its own genes
The capsid proteins themselves fold into it
The capsid takes it from a membrane of the host it infected
The host's immune cells attach it as a tag

items.explain: The envelope is acquired by the capsid from a cellular membrane in the host.

items.prompt: A virus has entered a cell and starts replicating. How does it get the new subunits for its capsids?

options.label: They are built using the cell's own protein-making machinery
They are carried in whole inside the infecting virus
The virus builds them in its own tiny factories
They are borrowed from the cell's wall

items.explain: New capsid subunits are synthesized using the protein biosynthesis mechanism of the host cell.

items.prompt: Why must a virus build a stable protein shell around its genes?

options.label: To give the virus the energy it needs to replicate
To make the particle larger than the cell it infects
To let the host's immune cells grab hold of it
To shield the genome from extremes of pH or temperature and from enzymes

items.explain: The shell protects the genome from lethal chemical and physical agents, including extremes of pH or temperature and proteolytic and nucleolytic enzymes.

items.prompt: Some complex viruses with double-stranded DNA assemble an empty shell first. How does the DNA get inside?

options.label: Through a specialized portal at one vertex of the shell
The shell is built around the DNA as the proteins co-assemble
The DNA seeps in through gaps between the shell proteins
The shell dissolves and re-forms around the DNA

items.explain: Such viruses assemble empty procapsids with a specialized portal structure at one vertex, and the viral DNA is translocated in through it.

items.prompt: A farmer's plants carry a rod-shaped, filamentous virus. Which capsid symmetry do many such plant viruses have?

options.label: Icosahedral symmetry
A cylinder with a cap at either end
Helical symmetry
No symmetry at all

items.explain: Many rod-shaped and filamentous plant viruses have capsids with helical symmetry.
